book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way
essays: Men in Bright Tights and Wild Fights, Often at Great Heights, and, of Course,
The One Question I Could Not Answer
Defining a Hero and a Superhero
What We Want and What We Get
Truth, Justice, and the American Way
Look On My Works, Ye Mighty
samples: The editors' introduction surveys the current resurgence of the superhero: Spider-Man's record-breaking opening weekends, 87,000 fans at the San Diego Comicon, and superhero references running through Seinfeld, Scrubs, rock, and rap. It argues that classic superhero stories, like the works of Plato and Aristotle, are here to stay - enduring modern myths that are wildly fun yet thought-provoking, with Superman and Batman now recognized worldwide as cultural icons.

The editors argue that superhero comics, an original American art form like jazz, deserve serious intellectual attention because they dramatize philosophy's deepest questions - ethics, responsibility, justice, personal identity, faith, friendship, and family. They press the point into the near future: genetic engineering and nanotechnology may soon make real the questions comics have long explored, such as whether to genetically supercharge a baby or what to do if you woke up with powers yourself. The volume brings philosophy professors together with comic-book writers and editors to wrestle with these issues.

Comic writer Mark Waid, hired by DC editor Dan DiDio to re-imagine Superman in Superman: Birthright, is stumped by the question 'Why does he do what he does?' He argues that post-9/11 kids see the Big Blue Boy Scout as an ultraconservative protector of a corrupt status quo, making him irrelevant to a generation that knows heroes from metal detectors and assassinated visionaries. Invoking Socrates' claim that the genuine search for wisdom begins with admitting we do not know, Waid resolves to unlearn a lifetime of Superman lore, and locates the key to the character's motivation in Kal-El's utter aloneness: he is the sole survivor of Krypton and 'doesn't belong here'.

Working out Birthright's answer, Waid argues that even the solar-powered Kal-El shares the human need to belong, so he can connect with humanity not by hiding his alien side but by embracing it. Echoing a Marianne Williamson passage about our fear of being 'powerful beyond measure', Waid has Superman wear the S-shield - the banner of his Kryptonian 'tribe' - and use his powers openly, because only by living authentically in service of others does he truly belong. He links this to Aristotle's discovery that happiness is rooted in living with excellence, which Superman 'in his own way' found too.

Waid closes by drawing out the paradox that Superman's shining selflessness is achieved through acting in his own self-interest: in saving others he exercises his distinctive powers and fulfills his authentic destiny, which fulfills him, while embracing his own nature and history puts him in the one activity that most helps others. There is no blanket choice between self and community, he argues - properly fulfilling one's own nature redounds to everyone's benefit - and Superman thereby becomes a mirror for examining the balance of selflessness and self-interest in the reader's own life.

Loeb and Morris take on the argument that 'superhero' is an oxymoron - the more super (and invulnerable) a being, the less it risks, so the less heroic it can be, which would disqualify Superman except under Kryptonite. They rebut it by insisting heroism is a moral category: a hero is a person of noble character whose worthy achievements are guided by the good, so a superhero is a person of noble character with superhuman powers or superhumanly developed abilities, which gets Batman and Green Arrow into the fray. They extend heroism to everyday firefighters, nurses, and stay-at-home mothers, and use J. Jonah Jameson's resentment of Spider-Man to show how the hero's sacrifice stands as a standing rebuke to spectators' inertia.

book: 014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche
samples: The editors' introduction argues that dieting — not just food — deserves philosophical attention, and that the Atkins Diet specifically raises 'chewy' questions about how to decide what to eat, what to believe, and whom to believe, precisely because it defies balanced-diet convention and much expert opinion. It opens with Plato's Republic prescription of roasted meats for campaigning guardians (no pots to carry), cites Nietzsche's Ecce Homo and its 'lengthy disquisition' on his own dietary choices as the rare philosophical treatment of diet, and credits Feuerbach with 'Der Mensch ist was er isst' — you are what you eat. It closes by mapping the volume's sixteen essays across Kant, Hume, Nietzsche, Marx, Dewey, environmental and feminist philosophy, critical race theory, and the philosophy of science.

Auxier, an Atkins dieter, argues the diet works for the reason Dewey gives in Human Nature and Conduct: habits built in calm moments are the bulwark against desire in crisis, and Atkins succeeds by reshaping which gratifications are habitually available — 'a steak for the black eye of desire.' He then transfers Atkins's physiology to thinking: television and advertising serve 'conceptual carbs,' packaged bundles of doubt, emotion, and readiness to act that bypass inquiry and leave the public 'intellectually diabetic' and ideological. Peirce's pragmatic maxim is translated into an eight-step mental exercise (worked through a parent's tattoo-or-piercing doubt about a teenage daughter), while Descartes's hyperbolic doubt is discarded in favor of pragmatism's 'genuine doubt.'

Framed by The Onion's 'New Nietzschian Diet Lets You Eat Whatever You Fear Most' and its 'Fat is dead' riff on the death of God, Irwin argues via Nietzsche's Ecce Homo that 'small things — nutrition, place, climate' matter more than philosophy usually admits, and that dieting belongs to giving style to one's character: we are both artists and works of art, so a 'sound mind in an Atkins body' is self-creation. Drawing on his own two years on the diet (187 to 165 pounds, steadier mood, lower cholesterol), he contends Atkins fits some constitutions — Schwarzenegger's carnivorous persona — and not others: Tony Soprano, devouring gabagool amid agita and fainting spells, could not do Atkins without ceasing to be who he is. Nietzsche's 'One has to know the size of one's stomach' becomes the rule of dietary self-knowledge.

Dennis uses Kant to sort eaters into the fundamentally unfree (Herbert, raised on Atkins and thieving, who merely ploughs on), the fundamentally random (Rita, whose synapses and muscles would fire in chaos), and the autonomous, arguing that only an autonomous person can genuinely decide whether to follow Atkins — by weighing friends' testimonials against the medical establishment rather than habit, whim, or advertising. The categorical imperative grounds the autonomous life: 'lie when you can gain' fails universalization, and treating humanity as an end means offering a vegetarian guest food she is comfortable with instead of pressing Atkins meat on her. His own 'Dan Dennis Diet,' built by experiment and reasoning, illustrates autonomy in practice, and the case of Kitty shows that observing someone's diet never reveals whether its holder is unfree or autonomous.

Knight places Atkins's caveman utopia — Paleolithic abundance, hunter-gatherer vitality, downfall through agriculture — inside the primitivist tradition running from Ovid's Golden Age to Rousseau's Noble Savage, whose state of nature Rousseau himself admitted was 'mere conditional and hypothetical reasoning' aimed at European corruption. Using postcolonial critics (Spurr, Torgovnick, and Fanon's line that whites who feel 'too mechanized' turn to 'the men of color' for 'human sustenance'), she argues low-carb primitivism is self-reflexive nostalgia — South Beach cannot even date its own paradise — that also freezes living Inuit and Indigenous Australians as Stone Age remnants, hiding the colonial and economic causes of their diabetes and poverty.

O'Connell extracts Brillat-Savarin's 1825 anti-flour-and-starch regimen — clear soup without croutons, shun beer, rye over white bread — as a 'proto-Atkins' and reconstructs its real argument: farmers fatten livestock on starches, so by Humean 'species of Analogy' starches fatten humans, from which abstinence from floury foods is 'deduced.' Hume's Enquiry Section IX, 'Of the Reason of Animals,' supplies the philosophical audit, distinguishing relations of ideas from matters of fact and grading the animal-to-human analogical inference as probable at best. The chapter ends with Hume's fork turned on the diet-book shelf: any volume without experiential reasoning concerning matter of fact deserves the flames — 'nothing but sophistry and illusion.'

samples: Jerry Walls's introduction opens with the film Shadowlands (the Oxford dons teasing Lewis about the fur coats in the wardrobe) to present Lewis as a part-time philosopher who taught philosophy at Oxford and presided over the Socratic Club. It previews the questions the Chronicles raise: truth versus illusion, whether might makes right, why be moral, what may be accepted on faith, whether more than one religion could be true, whether time flows differently in different worlds, and whether Eustace could become a dragon and still be the same person. It reassures Narnia fans that the essays enrich rather than ponderously distort ('gas') stories that should first be enjoyed on their own terms.

Stephen Webb argues that Lewis gives hearing, not sight, the fundamental role in knowledge: the Dufflepuds choose invisibility over ugliness, the crew in the Dark Island hear nightmares they cannot see, and in The Magician's Nephew Aslan is heard singing before he is seen. Against A.J. Ayer's logical positivism, Webb develops a 'vocative philosophy of sound' in which meaning lives in voices: Jadis's destructive Deplorable Word versus Aslan's world-creating song, Uncle Andrew's tone-deafness to warranted authority, and Shasta in The Horse and His Boy learning who he is from the voice in the dark that answers 'Myself.'

Kevin Kinghorn uses virtue epistemology (Sosa, Code) to solve the puzzle of why Uncle Andrew alone hears only roaring when Aslan sings Narnia into being: he fails all four intellectual virtues. He does not value truth for its own sake (unlike Frank the Cabby), indulges wishful thinking (like Edmund defending the Witch for Turkish Delight, or imagining Jadis fancies him), lets fear dictate belief (terror of the animals he has vivisected), and lacks Socratic self-knowledge, which the dragonized Eustace painfully acquires. A closing reading of Prince Caspian has each character's ability to see Aslan track their earlier trust in Lucy's testimony: sin blinds, and faith produces its own authenticating evidence.

Thomas Senor turns the Professor's trilemma about Lucy (lying, mad, or telling the truth) into a general account of when to believe incredible testimony: weigh the testifier's reliability against how well the claim fits your background beliefs. He shows why Lucy's siblings should have believed her second report of Aslan in Prince Caspian, since by then talking animals and a resurrected Lion no longer clashed with what they knew, and then applies the framework to 'Julia's' report of hearing God, arguing that believing, disbelieving, or withholding rationally depends on the hearer's own background commitments. A footnote explains why Hume on miracles does not fit Lucy's case, since she claims no violation of natural law.

Steven Lovell reads the Green Witch's enchantment in The Silver Chair (the sun is only a copy of the lamp, Aslan only a bigger cat, Narnia a children's tale) as Lewis's staging of the Freudian critique of religion, and answers that similarity cannot tell copy from original, that the genetic fallacy vitiates arguing from a belief's origin, and that Aslan is 'not safe,' so Christianity is hardly wish-fulfillment (Augustine's restless heart and Pascal's God-shaped hole point the other way). Puddleglum's stamping out the fire and vow to live 'as like a Narnian as I can even if there isn't any Narnia' is defended through Pascal's Wager and James's 'The Will to Believe': the reality of Narnia is a live, forced, and momentous option that may legitimately be decided on passional grounds.

Bruce Reichenbach recounts the failure of the Enlightenment quest for certainty from Descartes and Locke through Kant to the positivists, and argues that Lewis's Narnia instead models knowing as perspectival (the Stable door whose inside is bigger than its outside), value-laden (the Dwarfs' self-chosen dark paradigm that turns Aslan's feast into refuse and violets into stable litter), and personal (Lucy's unarguable knowledge that she has seen Aslan in Prince Caspian, read through Michael Polanyi's tacit knowledge). Kuhn's competing paradigms frame theism versus atheism, James's will to believe opens the chapter, and Plantinga's defeaters keep personal knowledge from collapsing into mere subjectivity.

essays: From Rhyme to Reason This Shit Ain’t Easy
Hip Hop and “This Makin’ Dollars Shit”
No Love (for Hip Hop), No problem
The Possibility of Authenticity The Life We Choose
The Hunger for More Than Serious Play
Hip-Hop Lyrics No Black CNN and No Art of Storytelling
Final Skit Paris’s Field Nigga Boogie
samples: Cornel West argues that Plato's dialogues invented philosophy as a Socratic genre of cross-examination and bold frank speech (parrhesia) about ordinary life, and that hip-hop music - like the spirituals, blues, and jazz - enacts that same parrhesia against conventional morality and entrenched power. He claims reading hip hop philosophically demands metaphilosophical subtlety, showing how paideia, phronesis, and parrhesia operate in the work of cultural producers under free-market fundamentalism and authoritarianism. Because the racial dimension of hip hop is inescapable, he says philosophers must break their discipline's silence on race and music (neglected figures like Du Bois and Alain Locke alongside Aristotle, Kant, and Rorty), closing with Cicero's Socrates who turned philosophy from the heavens to earth and William James's pragmatism that took it from the academy to the streets.

The editors' introduction argues that hip hop and philosophy are both street-born examinations of life in pursuit of wisdom: Socrates's elenchus is likened to MC lyrical battles and call-and-response (his interrogations compared to Rakim's technique, his execution for corrupting the youth to the fate of a controversial rapper), while Plato's philosopher-king parallels Kurtis Blow and Run-D.M.C. claiming thrones. After a Bronx hip-hop history sketch (Kool Herc, BDP's "The Bridge is Over"), they frame the volume around hip hop's suppressed fifth element of knowledge and preview its pairings: Aquinas and Rakim on God, Plato and Lauryn Hill on love, Sartre and Lil' Kim's gaze, Kant and Ice Cube on punishment, Hegel and Nas, Hobbes and Dead Prez, Mill and Chappelle on epithets. Record companies don't own hip hop and universities don't own philosophy, they conclude - both belong to whoever understands, loves, and respects them.

Framed by Rakim's "The Mystery" and Five-Percenter knowledge-of-self, Darby asks who God is and attacks divine omnipotence with the "paradox of the blunt" and "paradox of the glock" - can God roll a blunt so strong even he can't hit it? - then defends Aquinas's Summa Theologica restriction of God's power to the logically possible, against Descartes's claim that God can do even the impossible. He presses further with Tupac's jailbreak paradox from a Vibe interview ("If you God, then pop the fuckin' gate") and Aquinas's paradox of sin, resolving them via Samuel Clarke's natural/moral contradiction distinction and Socrates's Crito arguments for why a perfectly good person refuses escape and accepts the state's verdict.

Shelby stages Plato's Symposium as a cipher of raps on love to answer hip-hop "love haters" like Jay-Z ("I got ninety-nine problems but a bitch ain't one"): Pausanias's vulgar versus spiritual love, Aristophanes's myth of split halves read through Method Man and Mary J. Blige's "You're All I Need" and Biggie's "Me & My Bitch", and Socrates's ladder from beautiful bodies to Beauty itself, with Lauryn Hill's "Zion" as birth of beautiful offspring. He objects that Socrates makes the beloved a replaceable means to the good, and argues that Alcibiades's drunken confession supplies what is missing - love's possession, exclusivity, reciprocity, and drama (The Roots: "lies come in, that's where the drama begins") - concluding that love ain't just 'bout da booty but demands a vulnerability the love hater rightly fears.

Green reads Del tha Funkee Homosapien's line on Gorillaz's "Clint Eastwood" ("you don't see with your eye, you perceive with your mind") alongside Descartes's Meditations window passage - judging men in the square from hats and coats - to argue against the sense-data picture that perception is mind-guided, interest-driven interpretation rather than passive reception. He then deploys the "new" adaptive unconscious (the cocktail party effect, the love-on-the-bridge misattribution of arousal, unconscious racism in housing audits, lottery winners no happier - "mo money, mo problems") to show we are strangers to ourselves, so the proper use of the mind means standing back from one's patterns, as 2Pac's "Letter 2 My Unborn" and KRS-One's "The Mind" urge.

Pittman argues the rap battle - UTFO's "Roxanne, Roxanne" answered by Roxanne Shanté's "Roxanne's Revenge", Run-D.M.C.'s "Sucker MC's", Jay-Z's "Takeover" versus Nas's "Ether" - is hip hop's enactment of Hegel's master-slave struggle for recognition, where self-consciousness proves itself only through an all-or-nothing contest ending in domination rather than destruction. Gangsta rap (N.W.A's "Gangsta Gangsta", Ice Cube's fantasy raid on the suburbs) radicalizes the battle into a collective demand that America recognize black urban conditions, and the chapter turns to Du Bois's race-centered and Marx's class-centered revisions of Hegel's history to read "this makin' dollars shit" - Wu-Tang's "C.R.E.A.M.", Talib Kweli on capitalism and crack, Mos Def's "The Rape Over" - as the dialectic's capture of the cipher by corporate beef.

book: 017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)
essays: Love Minus Zero, No Limit or Going, Going Gone
The Ends of Despair From “Things Have Changed” to “Love and Theft”
Both Sides of Dylan and Politics
Man Gave a Name to a Lake
samples: Doug Anderson reads Dylan's Planet Waves as a modern Symposium: each song stages a rung on Diotima's ladder, from the puppy love of "You Angel You" through the physical eros of "Tough Mama" and "Hazel," the agape of "Forever Young," and the complementary true love of "Wedding Song." Like Socrates refusing Alcibiades in "Going, Going Gone," Dylan abandons finite beloveds because his highest eros is the creative act itself - poets achieve the immortality Diotima demands by giving birth to immortal works rather than children. The chapter argues both Plato and Dylan finally define love as desire for truth and beauty that outlasts any particular relationship.

Rick Furtak traces an existential arc through Dylan's later albums, reading Blood on the Tracks ("Tangled Up in Blue," "You're a Big Girl Now") as Camus's absurd divorce between a mind that cares and a world that has gone silent, and Heideggerian care as what the narrator loses in "Simple Twist of Fate." "Brownsville Girl" and "Most of the Time" embody Kierkegaard's knight of infinite resignation - hope abandoned but the precious past never forgotten - while "Not Dark Yet" and "Things Have Changed" mark the nadir of despair. On Love and Theft ("Mississippi," "Sugar Baby") the singer turns toward an absurd, Kierkegaardian faith that keeps caring and even loves without demanding that life make sense.

Avery Kolers uses "Only a Pawn in Their Game" and its companion "Who Killed Davey Moore?" to argue that Dylan treats Byron de la Beckwith as a pawn: a poor white duped by divide-and-rule tactics, the psychological wage of whiteness, shame, and lynch-mob indoctrination into fearing a Hobbesian war of all against all. Against Aristotle's account of acting in ignorance, the chapter asks whether Beckwith's ignorance of his real enemies was culpable, concluding his bad moral luck (in Bernard Williams's sense) was manufactured by white supremacy and so reflects back on all white people. Dylan's refusal to name or voice Beckwith adopts Strawson-style objective attitudes, making blaming itself a political act aimed at the system rather than the shooter.

James Klagge, defining terms in Socratic fashion, distinguishes bootlegs like Great White Wonder from piracy and argues unreleased Dylan material (the New York Blood on the Tracks, "Blind Willie McTell," the 1966 Live concert) has genuine musical and historical value. He rejects the Sophist view that morality is just self-interest and the relativist "everybody's doing it" defense, then weighs the artist's Lockean property and privacy rights against fans' rights of access, noting legal-but-immoral and illegal-but-moral cases in the spirit of Martin Luther King's civil disobedience. His verdict: bootlegging is morally acceptable when royalties are fair, stolen tapes are not used, and mainly public performances circulate.

Krein and Levin read Dylan's portraits of fallen socialites in "Like a Rolling Stone," "Just Like a Woman," and "To Ramona" as critiques of bad faith - characters who hide from freedom and responsibility in consumerist status games, in Sartre's sense that existence precedes essence. But Beauvoir's Second Sex exposes the cost: the women Dylan praises ("Girl from the North Country," "One More Cup of Coffee") are praised precisely for staying in immanent, pastoral passivity, denied the transcendence that for Beauvoir constitutes full humanity. Borrowing Benjamin's and Buck-Morss's notion of modern "dreamworlds," they finally read Dylan's pastoral utopias as a counter-dreamworld spun after the collapse of the mass-utopian promise of consumer happiness.

Jordy Rocheleau reads Dylan's protest era ("The Lonesome Death of Hattie Carroll," "Hurricane," "Chimes of Freedom") as Enlightenment social criticism in Kant's and Mill's sense: reason can expose injustice and secure autonomy against majority tyranny. The post-protest Dylan ("My Back Pages," "Desolation Row," "It's Alright, Ma") turns postmodern - Lyotard's incredulity toward metanarratives, Derrida's ever-deferred meanings, and Foucault's power/knowledge, where ideals of freedom become instruments of domination. Yet Dylan keeps crying for justice ("Political World," "Dignity"), so the chapter concludes postmodern skepticism can only serve as a cautionary check within, not a replacement of, Enlightenment politics - the thief's line in "All Along the Watchtower" as commitment amid confusion.

Foreword by R.K. Stratman, a self-made motorcycle-race T-shirt vendor whose family business grew from iron-on patches at the races to a company of over two hundred employees. He recounts his first ride in a high-school parking lot, his collection of first-and-last engine models including the Buffalo Bike, and names the allure of the ride: freedom on the open road, escape from conformity, and the instant brotherhood of riders whose image has become a pop-culture stereotype. His only contribution to the philosophy of Harley-Davidson is his company's twenty-year slogan: 'If I have to explain, you wouldn't understand.'

Editor Bernard Rollin frames the book with his Yellowstone anecdote: dreading the 'Dreaded Question' about his profession, he confesses to an outlaw biker that he is a philosophy professor and is embraced with 'You have a steady job so you can keep the bike running!' He draws two morals: Harley riders share an instant camaraderie (the trauma surgeon who cursed him for costing him a ride) plus a quiet elitism of being privy to something most people never experience, and bikers treat everything, even careers, as ancillary to time on the motorcycle. The book's essays aim to explain this je ne sais quoi of the Harley way of life.

Priest argues that Pirsig's Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance is far more genuinely Zen than its disclaimer admits: once riding becomes effortless, the dissolution of the subject-object distinction that Dogen calls genjokoan arrives on the open road ('you ARE the driving and the road and the elements'), and the Harley's relaxed posture and low-revving thug-thug-thug rhythm make it a better vehicle for suchness than cars or whinier bikes. Even maintenance done as an end in itself is genjokoan, and because ultimate reality erases every conceptual distinction, care of self, others, and the bike amount to the same thing, the Mahayana ground of compassion; the mountain-and-water Zen saying resolves the paradox that the unconceptualized and the conceptualized are one. Suffering, on the Buddhist diagnosis Priest applies, comes from imposing conceptual grids that see the world wrong, and seeing it aright dissolves it.

Auxier uses the question 'Would Bruce Springsteen ride a Honda?' as an ontological probe: Honda embodies defensible middle-class values while a Harley is not primarily a machine but 'a decision about life and what makes it valuable', a suicide machine Jesus could have ridden into Jerusalem and whose absence would render Easy Rider meaningless even if Fonda rode some other Harley. His own boyhood purchase of a Honda XL 70 over the Harley Z90 becomes a lesson in Heideggerian honesty, since he knew he belonged on a Honda, while buyers who choose for appearances are consumed by das Man, the they-self that lives inauthentically through images and slogans. Using Husserl's method of imaginative variation on the question, he concludes that the Harley as cultural icon represents an existential decision and the life that follows from it.

Over an evening at the Iron Post biker bar, Auxier maps four habitues onto the Hellenistic schools: Cowboy, the Vietnam chopper pilot whose bar is a Garden of modest pleasures, loyalty, and withdrawal from power games, is an Epicurean; the laconic Bear, who doubts that even possessing knowledge would make us better off and suspends judgment, is a Pyrrhonian (unlike the coffee-house Carneadean); Happy Jack, the 'true nature's child' of 'Born to Be Wild' who defies convention and keeps nothing six months, is Diogenes's Cynic; and Gary, the Vietnam-damaged recovering alcoholic, is a damaged Stoic who has not reached apatheia. He concludes that bikers are postmodern pagans whose philosophy is enacted rather than propounded, a Biker Platonism that refuses the Christian-Platonic divorce of body and spirit and lives by honor, freedom, and a pagan fatalism that accepts the consequences of one's choices.

Goldstein applies Hegel's thesis-antithesis-synthesis and Marx's more complex, multidimensional dialectic to the splits within biker culture: bar-room stare-downs as struggles for recognition, wrenchers versus trailers, RUBs versus working-class riders, helmet disputes, and one-percenters versus the rest. He traces the collapse of brotherhood (the clenched fist of solidarity giving way to the selective wave) to the commodification of the motorcycle during the Japanese invasion and to Harley's own yuppie-era Willie G. marketing, arguing via commodity fetishism that bikers misread economic forces between manufacturers as personal differences. His conclusion is that the seeds of unity lie within the divisions, and that Harley-Davidson Motor Co. will not save the culture, since its task is profit, not tradition.

book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!
essays: And Where the @#$%^& is the Queen
“Life’s a Piece of Shit” The Question of Heroism
Suppose You Were Attached to a Dead Parrot The Role of Thought Experiments
Getting Right with Brian (Just in Case)
Yes, but What About the Killer Rabbit
Prayer (A Euphemism for Butt-Kissing and Begging)
The Epilogue A Question of Belief
Knowledge and Nihilism Science and Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life
So, What Have Philosophers Ever Done for Us
No Shoes for Muskrats How the 1956 Olympic Games Destroyed Indonesian Art
samples: The editors' introduction recounts Monty Python's 1969 debut and argues the troupe's absurdism bears a deep connection to philosophy because the British Pythons absorbed the Oxford and Cambridge linguistic analysis of Russell, Wittgenstein, Moore, and Ryle while at university in the 1960s. It tours the volume's three parts, previewing each contributor's pairing: Schilbrack reading Life of Brian through Camus's absurd hero, Brighouse using the Argument Clinic for Rawls's analysis of social practices, Asma finding Buddhist mindfulness in The Meaning of Life, Huss pairing the Pythons with Hume on religion, and Spinelli reading sketches through Foucault on the social construction of madness. It concludes there is no single connection between Python and philosophy but many: sketches illuminate philosophy, philosophy illuminates sketches, and Python's empire says something about philosophy's cultural standing (with Wittgenstein's duck-rabbit figuring how the remaining chapters can be seen).

Argues Life of Brian is heretical rather than blasphemous: it never mocks Jesus or belief in God but ridicules gullible, smug believing — the Sermon on the Mount crowd mishearing 'blessed are the cheesemakers,' the sandal schism — a critique the chapter aligns with Hume on the appetite for the marvelous and on anthropomorphism. It reads Brian's window sermon ('You're all individuals... think for yourselves') as Kant's Sapere aude and as an existentialist, possibly Christian, humanism. Against the charge of nihilism, it places Brian squarely in Camus's absurd universe (the pointless crucifixion finale and 'Always Look on the Bright Side of Life') and asks whether Brian is an absurd hero like Sisyphus, Meursault, or Dr. Rieux; he is not — he never scorns his fate — so the chapter proposes 'absurd decent guy': Brian lives sincerely, without waiting for miracles, and humor rather than revolt is the counterweight to absurdity.

Asks how the exploding-glutton Mr. Creosote sequence in 'The Autumn Years' of The Meaning of Life can provoke laughter rather than horror, given that Creosote shares the monster's marks of physiological impossibility and disgusting category-violation (like Frankenstein's monster or the Alien). The answer: horror requires disgust plus fear, and Creosote, like the slapstick clown, is marked as neither able to harm nor be harmed, so the audience's fear-condition for horror is never met. A second layer of the laughter is vindictive: the maitre d''s wafer-thin mint is retributive justice, a morality-play punishment for gluttony in the lineage of Spenser's Gluttony and Dante's Inferno, so black comedy trades on our sense that the victim deserves what he gets.

Uses 'Piston Engine (a Bargain)' from the Hamlet episode of Flying Circus — park-bench women who buy gift-wrapped piston engines because 'it was a bargain,' kill birds with hurled groceries, and end by dazedly reciting Hamlet — to test Wittgenstein's theories of meaning. Both the early Verification Principle and the later meaning-as-use principle fail: we understand the meaning of every sentence yet cannot make sense of what the women are saying, just as 'This is my hand' at the doctor's office, or the philosopher's 'I know that that's a tree' (Wittgenstein's joke at Moore's expense), is meaningful but senseless in context. Drawing on Remarks on Colour and On Certainty, Smith concludes that communal practices and forms of life fix what it makes sense to say, and that the sketch proves Python's Horatio point — 'there are more things in heaven and earth than are dreamt of in your philosophy' — since no theory of meaning captures what makes the exchange funny.

Takes the Argument Clinic sketch — Mr. Vibrating's pure contradiction versus the customer's demand for 'a connected series of statements intended to establish a proposition' — to argue that paying for good argument is not absurd, because only sustained argument with others gets most of us true beliefs about complex matters. It explains Rawls's method of reflective equilibrium (testing general principles against considered judgments about cases, illustrated by the author's Rimbaud/Rambo censorship blunder) and Judith Jarvis Thomson's violinist thought experiment, showing how such experiments force us to abandon groundless reasons: opponents of abortion who let the violinist go must find grounds other than the fetus's right to life. Good thought experiments, it closes, work like good Python sketches — the Dead Parrot sketch's internally logical absurdity — so a real argument clinic would serve a genuine social function, since interlocutors expose biases that solitary reflection cannot.

Reads Life of Brian through Nietzsche's madman: the crowd's laughter at Brian's market sermons ('consider the lilies... have the birds got jobs?') enacts the death of the cheerless, pathos-soaked God, with Brian as a sincere 'divine idiot' who escapes ressentiment by falling idiotically below the dialectic rather than rising above it as an Übermensch. Bergson's account of the comic — rigidity invisible to its bearer, 'as though wearing the ring of Gyges with reverse effect' — explains why the Pythons' straight men, British class consciousness, and the Roman/British empires ('Romani ite domum,' the centurion's Latin lesson) are funny, and why Britons and Romans can laugh at themselves while Americans cannot. Pivoting from Jorge's war on laughter in Eco's The Name of the Rose, the chapter closes with a Pascal's-wager parody: having laughed at Brian, you have already wagered your immortal soul on God being British — the sort of God who can take a joke.

book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings
samples: The editor's introduction stages poker and philosophy as twin crafts of risk: 'philosopher' was once slang for a card cheat, Socrates and Wild Bill Hickok both died for keeping villainous company, and the Buddha's six years to enlightenment are measured against the Birdcage Theater's eight-year poker game. It recruits Nietzsche's 'live dangerously' and Kierkegaard's leap of faith to defend the all-in as the only meaningful way to live, then traces probability from Cardano's Book on Games of Chance to Pascal's wager that believing in God is the smarter bet — the ancestor of today's pot-odds reasoning. Chris Ferguson's PhD, Annie Duke's psycholinguistics, and Jesse May's 'the trick to poker is mastering the luck — that's philosophy' set up the book's Texas Hold'em focus.

Ventimiglia mines No-Limit Hold'em for seven lessons philosophers also teach: we lack certain knowledge (Descartes' cogito is the famous quest for certainty, but philosophy's own history of disagreement proves uncertainty is the human condition), and like William James against Clifford we must still believe and act without the nuts — waiting for pocket aces while the blinds eat you alive is no strategy. Risking everything echoes Thoreau's escape from lives of quiet desperation, trusting hunches over arithmetic follows Thoreau and Peirce's sentimentalism, and the Darwin-and-Spencer competition of tournament poker hides a deeper cooperative social contract: get caught cheating and you are out of the game. It closes with Plato's four classic virtues from the Republic — wisdom, courage, moderation, and the justice of a balanced soul — as the perfection of a poker player.

Belliotti tells of busting 'Pickle Puss' with flopped queens and of tight 'Howard the Vest' paying off his flopped full house to ask whether Marx's diagnoses — alienation in four forms, exploitation of surplus value, and false consciousness spread through the ideological superstructure by the economic base — condemn poker. He argues no: unlike coerced factory labor, poker is freely chosen creative activity that energizes our species-being like an absorbed artist, as Doyle 'Texas Dolly' Brunson's road-gambler career and his famous ten-deuce full-house call against Jessie Alto at the 1976 WSOP (and the 1980 loss to Stu Ungar's gutshot) show. Poker may still launder capitalist ideology — antes that lure investment, zero-sum rivalry, rugged individualism — but the owner-worker exploitation Marx feared has no equivalent at an equal-buy-in table.

Young reads David Sklansky's fundamental theorem of poker — play as if you could see all the cards — through Aristotle and Husserl. Aristotle's phronesis and virtue-as-habituation explain how excellent players come to perceive the particulars (pot odds, opponent tendencies, the best possible hand) and stay unharmed even when losing with the best play, while Husserl's Cartesian Meditations, translated hand-by-hand into poker terms, supply analogical appresentation for knowing the other minds seated across the table. Chris Moneymaker's 2003 'Bluff of the Century' all-in with nothing against Sammy Farha shows how bluffing randomizes play and lets you shape the truth you seek, until a slow-played quad aces ends the night in Socratic humility about the limits of knowledge.

Sanders splits poker into two philosophical styles. The Rationalist — Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason, Pascal's domestication of chance into probability — plays like Sklansky, Chris Ferguson, and Howard Lederer, whose temptation is the paralysis of analysis; the Existentialist — Sartre's existence precedes essence, Camus' scorn for the absurd, Kierkegaard's leap of faith taken without decisive evidence — plays like Gus Hansen calling Antonio Esfandiari's $334,000 all-in re-raise with ten-high. A Russell-and-Popper-style regress of predictions (knowing a prediction changes its outcome) becomes the tournament 'hall of mirrors' of intentions read in Phil Ivey and Johnny Chan, and the chapter lands on Richard Taylor's existentialist point that meaning comes from committed doing, at the table as in life.

Vernezze uses Dostoevsky to make gambling existential: Notes from Underground's insistence that will trumps reason ('what do I care for the laws of nature and arithmetic?') and The Gambler's portrait of the calculating gambler — who loses like everyone else and worships money with a 'German' soul — prefigure existentialism's three traits: lost confidence in reason, despair as part of the human condition, and the willed overcoming of absurdity (Camus' Sisyphus happy, Sartre's condemned freedom). Dostoevsky's own roulette addiction fuels the reading, with Amarillo Slim and Brunson's side bets as heirs. The Cincinnati Kid's climax clinches it: Lancey Howard 'making the wrong move at the right time' by chasing a straight flush proves poker's essence lies beyond reason — a truly Dostoevskean activity.

book: 021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band
samples: Wrathall's introduction argues U2 is philosophically interesting because its enormous popularity holds up a mirror to what 'we' care about (by Nietzsche's test of how a culture stands toward life) and because the band publicly wrestles with the contradictions of the technological-global economy: unprecedented freedom of choice paired with loss of rooted identity, and distant suffering ('Crumbs from Your Table') that we feel both powerless to fix and responsible for. Its showcase reading treats 'Miracle Drug' as a musical theodicy: Bono's plea 'God, I need your help tonight' is answered by the Edge's guitar and by the Matthew 25:35 refrain, so science and medicine count as works of Christian charity. The piece then frames the volume's essays: Plato's ascent of love in the early songs, Kierkegaardian despair after Achtung Baby, Bono's search for authentic identity, the simulacra of 'Even Better than the Real Thing', being-toward-death in the apocalyptic songs, and the Plato-versus-Aristotle quarrel over music's emotional power.

McCoy reads U2's early longing songs through the Symposium: Aristophanes' split-beings myth turns 'New Year's Day' into a song about incompleteness whose separated lovers also stand for Poland under Soviet domination, and Diotima's ladder of love reads 'I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For' and 'City of Blinding Lights' as stages ascending from bodily beauty toward the soul and then to Beauty itself. Against a tragic reading, she argues that by Diotima's account the restless lover on the ascent 'begets' discourses and songs, so 'With or Without You' is a song of surrender rather than despair. October's 'Gloria' and 'With a Shout' get the Augustinian ending: the restless heart finds in God the object Romantic love never supplies.

Dreyfus and Wrathall read U2's head/heart split through Kierkegaard's Sickness unto Death: the Christian-Platonic strategy of escaping the earthly (the sun-blindness of 'Staring at the Sun', the ascent of 'Gone') collapses into despair once both sides of the self prove essential, while 'The Playboy Mansion' and 'Discotheque' depict Kierkegaardian leveling and spiritlessness in consumer culture and 'Last Night on Earth' the aesthetic-sphere despair of living pure possibility. Pascal's contradictory great-and-miserable self and Augustine's two cities supply the tradition U2 inherits, and Nietzsche's 'nihilism' names what U2 calls 'pop'. They close by arguing that Bono's pseudonymous stage characters (the Fly, MacPhisto) do phenomenology just as Kierkegaard's pseudonyms do, and that U2's songs about something missing bear out despair's 'dialectic of eternity'.

Wrathall reads 'Vertigo' through Heidegger's vertigo-before-a-question and Kierkegaard's account of despair as the dizziness of a self whose sensual and spiritual sides are both essential. He uses rock's own testimony - Rammstein's 'Engel' and 'Sehnsucht', Nine Inch Nails' 'Down in It' - to confirm the existentialist thesis that neither flesh nor spirit can be renounced, with Pascal's God-shaped void as the diagnosis. He then argues that 'Beautiful Day', 'When I Look at the World', 'Grace' and 'Mysterious Ways' sketch an existential Christianity in which faith is not propositional confidence but a world-disclosing skill acquired like any know-how, and in which concrete erotic love ('if you want to kiss the sky, better learn how to kneel', the girl with crimson nails who 'has Jesus round her neck') discloses God on earth.

Malpas takes The Joshua Tree as an album about place: its desert imagery and restless movement ('Where the Streets Have No Name', 'I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For' as 'an anthem of doubt more than faith') carry the listener from Ireland to Reagan's America to Pinochet's Chile, while its political references - Ethiopian famine, El Salvador, Dublin high-rises - always work through concrete locations rather than abstract ideals. Using Heidegger on homelessness as the inability to dwell, and Marx and Engels' 'all that is solid melts into air', he argues that modernity has not erased our relatedness to place but covered it over. The album's desolation is therefore readable the other way: belonging is constituted through care, commitment and uncertain journeying in the places we already are ('Heartland').

Soper tracks Bono's public identity work across three paradigms: pre-modern Irish-Catholic inheritance, including a Du Boisian 'double consciousness' of the colonized Irish; the modernist artist-as-visionary, where Nietzsche, Freud and Marx destabilize the self and the Shalom fellowship nearly ends the band; and the postmodern masks of the Fly, Mirrorball Man and MacPhisto on the Zoo TV media collage, read via Lacan for 'Mofo' and via Baudrillard's simulacra for the 'Even Better than the Real Thing' video with its wax Beatles and cyber-sex imagery. Lyotardian skepticism toward grand ideologies explains the band's refusal of fanaticism in 'Sunday Bloody Sunday' and 'Two Hearts Beat as One'. Soper concludes that Bono fuses all three into a 'Postmodern Christian Pragmatism' that keeps Christian conviction and debt-relief activism while adopting postmodern playfulness without collapsing into ironic detachment.

book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless
essays: A New Lease of Life for the Undead
Not to Put Too Fine a Point on It
Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep
“Hey, Let’s Get the Stuff We Need!” Putting the Mall in Its Place
Universal Rights Vampires, Space Aliens, Robots, and Humans
The Possibility of a Non-Repressive Civilization
The Male Vampire as Metrosexual . . . Sort Of
samples: The editors' introduction surveys the twenty-first-century vampire and zombie boom (Twilight, True Blood, Zombieland, Fido, Pride and Prejudice and Zombies, Humans Versus Zombies, zombie walks) and asks why zombies specifically fascinate us. It proposes that the vampire embodies a Nietzschean super-humanity beyond good and evil, still charged with unheeded guilt, while the zombie is sub-Nietzschean: a Spinozan force of decomposition, a completely non-moral interaction of matter with other matter. Zombies work as hyperdead memento mori through which we imagine our own annihilation and our transformation into something posthuman, even as they are repackaged as one more consumer product distracting us from the very Real they reflect.

Richard Greene asks why becoming Undead is bad for the one who becomes Undead and why we rank it worse than death, restricting himself to unfriendly vampires and zombies (setting aside soulful exceptions like Angel, Spike, Louis, and Ed from Shaun of the Dead). He tests Nagel's deprivation view (vampires gain infinite experiences, so nothing is deprived) and Williams's desire-frustration view (undeath replaces rather than frustrates desires: scotch for blood, pork roast for raw flesh), then Mill's better-Socrates-dissatisfied comparison and the thought that the Undead's evil nature makes undeath objectively bad. Each fails, so he concludes undeath is not objectively bad, only comparatively bad, and one might as well make the best of it.

William Larkin uses Romero's films - Karen Cooper devouring her father in Night of the Living Dead, Roger begging Peter to shoot him in Dawn, Riley's 'Those people are all dead' in Land - to argue that persons are res corporealis, bodily continuers, rather than Descartes's res cogitans. Our terror of becoming a zombie ourselves and our grief at recognized neighbors in the horde reveal that deep down we think persons survive as corpses, so bodily continuity suffices for identity while psychological continuity is unnecessary. The Locke-style body-switching intuition (prince and cobbler) that supports the psychological approach is dismissed as theoretically biased data compared to what good zombie fiction draws out of us.

Hamish Thompson asks why we kill zombies with so few qualms and whether zombification releases us from obligations to the person who was, testing brain-death criteria, altered-identity and self-defense justifications against Shaun of the Dead (Shaun's mother and Ed), Day of the Dead's Bub, White Zombie, and Invasion of the Body Snatchers. He borrows Hume's bundle theory - the self as a fiction, a bundle of perceptions rather than an essence - and Parfit's degrees of psychological continuity to dissolve the sharp alive/dead and same-person/other-person dichotomies that make zombie-killing easy. The payoff is that we are already partly zombie (Shaun's checkout line, Ed on the sofa, the author's all-night gaming), differing only in our capacity for brief autonomous, goal-directed choices like Shaun's three-plan montage.

Manuel Vargas argues the Undead are not a natural kind but a nominal kind - vampires, zombies, and composite creatures like Frankenstein's monster share nothing except our classificatory practice - and that most actual Undead would probably be of natural origin (viruses, viroids, seeds, cryonics cases) rather than supernatural. He distinguishes philosophical zombies (Chalmers's conscious-less duplicates) from genuinely Undead beings, then defines malevolent evil as acting on a non-instrumental desire to harm others. On that definition zombies (mere appetite, like a deadly virus) and even vampires (whose damnation, contrary to early Buffy, need not add malicious motives) probably lack it, so if we ever meet the Undead they would be less likely to be evil than any random living person.

Larry Hauser stages the philosophy-of-mind zombie debate through Blade Runner's Replicants: Descartes's animal automata and his hats-and-coats worry about other minds, Turing's universal machines grounding functionalism, Kripke's necessity of scientific identifications (water is necessarily H2O), and Searle's silicon-chip replacement scenario show how zombies 'eat' behaviorist, functionalist, and identity-theoretic accounts of mind. He then deploys his own 'good zombies' - the beloved who might be a zombie, super-smart NEXUS 9s, venerable zombie thinkers - to block the dualist retreat on the cognitive side of the mind. The essay closes by doubting, with Chalmers's phenomenal zombies in view, that such zombies are coherently conceivable after all, and asks whether Deckard has been 'retiring' persons like Rachel all along.
